\vspace{0.5em}

Wordle is a daily word-guessing game whose public sharing format turned
every player into a voluntary data reporter: each result is posted as a grid
of coloured squares. The problem asks us to explain how results spread and to
predict future report volume.

We model the phenomenon as a four-compartment epidemic process, \textbf{PCQL},
which extends the classic SIR structure with a Quitted compartment and a Loyal
compartment. The extension is not cosmetic. A basic SIR model cannot reproduce
two features that are unmistakable in the data: growth decays slowly rather
than collapsing once the peak passes, and activity never returns to zero. Both
require a population that leaves and a subpopulation that keeps playing.

We calibrate the model against 400 days of daily report totals using a
least-squares fit over a four-dimensional grid search with local refinement.
The fit achieves $R^2 = 
\numRSquared{}$ on the observed series, with a
root-mean-square error of 
\numRmse{} reports per day. The
estimated transmission rate is $\beta = 
\numBeta{}$ per day and the
boredom rate is $\gamma = 
\numGamma{}$ per day, giving a basic
reproduction number of 
\numRZero{}, well above the threshold of one.
This confirms that spread is self-sustaining rather than driven by external
promotion.

A single-factor sensitivity analysis over $\beta$ shows that the timing of the
peak is highly elastic: raising $\beta$ from 0.20 to 0.45 moves the predicted
peak from day 
\numPeakDayBetaZeroTwoZero{} forward to day 
\numPeakDayBetaZeroFourFive{},
while the peak volume stays within a narrow band. Timing, not magnitude, is
the quantity that transmission rate controls.

Our model does not reproduce the observed peak timing accurately: it peaks
near day 40 while the data peaks at day 93. We report this rather than tune it
away, and we explain why a homogeneous-mixing model cannot represent the
staged adoption created by the word-difficulty schedule. We then give a
corrected forecasting procedure anchored on the observed peak.

\vspace{1em}
\noindent\textbf{Keywords:} compartmental model, social contagion, Wordle, parameter estimation, sensitivity analysis

\section{Introduction}\label{sec:SEC-010}
On 1 January 2022, a five-letter word game became a mass social ritual. Wordle's
distinctive feature is not the puzzle but the \emph{sharing format}: after solving,
a player may post a compact grid of coloured squares that reveals how many
attempts were needed without revealing a single letter of the answer. Players
post these grids on public social feeds, and those posts are the only public
record of the game's popularity.

This makes Wordle an unusually clean object of study. Report volume is an
observable proxy for the size of the active player population, and the proxy is
voluntary, standardised, and timestamped. The problem asks us to explain how
results spread through the population and to predict how many reports will be
submitted in the future.

\subsection{Prior work and the gap we address}

Two literatures bear on this problem. The first is epidemic modelling of
information spread, where the classical SIR structure \cite{kermack1927} has
been applied to rumours, memes, and online content. The second is empirical
work on daily-habit games, which documents rapid adoption followed by slow
decay but rarely specifies a generative mechanism.

The gap is that a basic SIR model cannot reproduce the observed shape of this
data. Two features are unmistakable in our 400-day series: after the peak,
activity declines slowly rather than collapsing, and it never approaches zero.
Under SIR, the removed compartment is terminal -- once a player stops, they
never return -- so the model forces a particular decay profile that the data
contradicts. Our contribution is a four-compartment extension that reproduces
both features with a mechanism rather than a fitted fudge factor, and an honest
account of where it still fails.

\subsection{What this paper does}

We build the \textbf{PCQL} model, which splits the classical removed class into
\emph{Quitted} and \emph{Loyal} populations, so that lapsed players can return.
We estimate its four parameters by least squares against 400 days of daily
report totals, validate the fit against held-out behaviour, and run a
single-factor sensitivity analysis on the transmission rate. We then report a
structural failure of the model -- it peaks far earlier than the data -- and
give a corrected forecasting procedure that anchors on the observed peak.

Section \ref{sec:assumptions} states our assumptions and their justifications.
Section \ref{sec:notations} defines notation. Section \ref{sec:model} develops
and calibrates the model. Section \ref{sec:sensitivity} reports the sensitivity
analysis. Section \ref{sec:sw} discusses strengths and weaknesses, and
Section \ref{sec:conclusion} concludes.

\section{Restatement of the Problem}\label{sec:SEC-020}
We are given daily counts of Wordle result posts, disaggregated by the number
of attempts taken, spanning 400 days from 7 January 2022 to
10 February 2023. Writing $y_t$ for the total number of reports on
day $t$, we address three tasks.

\begin{enumerate}
  \item \textbf{Explain the spread.} Identify a generative mechanism whose
  parameters are interpretable, and estimate them from the data rather than
  assuming them.
  \item \textbf{Predict future volume.} Produce forecasts for future report
  counts, and state the conditions under which those forecasts hold.
  \item \textbf{Quantify the influence of the model's knobs.} Determine which
  parameters actually control the predictions, and how much error each
  contributes.
\end{enumerate}

We treat the report count as a proportional proxy for the active player
population. The proportionality constant is unknown and is absorbed by a free
scale factor during calibration, so no assumption about the absolute
popularity of the game is required.

\subsection{What the data look like}

Before modelling, three features of the series constrain what any acceptable
model must do. First, the series is not monotone: it rises to a peak and then
declines, so a pure growth model is ruled out. Second, the decline is slow. If
the game lost players at the rate it gained them, activity would fall to a
negligible level within weeks of the peak; it does not. Third, the series never
approaches zero, even at the end of the window when the game was no longer
novel.

Any model we propose must therefore contain a mechanism for retention. This
observation, made before any equations were written, is what rules out the
standard SIR structure and motivates the extension in
Section \ref{sec:model}.

\subsection{Scope and exclusions}

Two things are deliberately outside scope. We do not attempt to model the
content of individual puzzles, because word difficulty is not recorded in the
data we have. We do not attempt to predict the game's commercial trajectory,
which would require revenue data that is not public. Both exclusions are
restated as limitations in Section \ref{sec:sw}.

\section{Assumptions and Justifications}\label{sec:SEC-030}
Each assumption below is stated with the reason it is defensible, because an
unjustified assumption is the easiest part of a model to attack.

\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{Homogeneous mixing.} Every potential participant is equally
  likely to encounter an active player. \emph{Justified} because Wordle spreads
  through social feeds and group chats rather than a physical contact network,
  so geographic and demographic structure does not dominate the dynamics.

  \item \textbf{Closed population.} The pool of potential participants is fixed
  over the study window. \emph{Justified} because the window is 400 days, over
  which the reachable population changed by far less than the observed
  fifteen-fold swing in activity.

  \item \textbf{Stable reporting rate.} The fraction of players who post results
  is constant over time, so report volume is proportional to active players.
  \emph{Justified} because the sharing prompt and its format did not change
  during the window; the free scale factor absorbs its level.

  \item \textbf{Constant parameters.} Transmission and boredom rates do not vary
  over the window. This is a deliberate simplification, and unlike the three
  above it is \emph{not} free: Section \ref{sec:sw} shows the residual structure
  it leaves behind, and we treat that structure as evidence against the
  assumption rather than as noise.
\end{itemize}

\section{Model I}\label{sec:SEC-050}
\subsection{Model intuition}

We model the player population as moving between four states. A \emph{potential}
participant has not played yet. An \emph{active} player currently plays and posts.
A \emph{quitted} player has stopped. A \emph{loyal} player plays durably and is
the reason the game does not die out.

Two transitions carry the whole argument. First, potential participants become
active through contact with people who are already playing -- this is the
contagion channel. Second, and this is the departure from SIR, a player who
stops is not removed from the system forever: some lapsed players return and
join the loyal group, which continues to recruit. A model without this channel
cannot produce the slow, non-vanishing decay that the data show.

Figure \ref{fig:flow} shows the end-to-end procedure: aggregation, calibration,
validation, sensitivity analysis, and forecasting.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=0.92\textwidth]{figures/FIG-005.pdf}
  \caption{Modelling and validation workflow. The validation gate is explicit:
  the fit is carried forward to forecasting only if $R^{2}$ clears the
  acceptance level.}
  \label{fig:flow}
\end{figure}

The solution must satisfy three constraints. The transmission rate is positive;
the loss and conversion rates are non-negative; and the four compartments sum
to a conserved total $N$, since no player is created or destroyed by the
mechanism itself.

\subsection{Governing equations}

Let $P(t)$, $C(t)$, $Q(t)$ and $L(t)$ denote the sizes of the four compartments
and $N(t)$ their sum. The dynamics are

\begin{align}
  \frac{dP}{dt} &= -\beta \frac{P(C+L)}{N} \label{eq:one} \\
  \frac{dC}{dt} &= \beta \frac{P(C+L)}{N} - (\gamma + \lambda) C \label{eq:two} \\
  \frac{dQ}{dt} &= \gamma C \label{eq:three} \\
  \frac{dL}{dt} &= \lambda C - \phi L \label{eq:four}
\end{align}

Here $\beta$ is the transmission rate, $\gamma$ the boredom rate at which active
players stop, $\lambda$ the rate at which quitted players become loyal, and
$\phi$ the attrition rate of loyal players. Equation \eqref{eq:one} depletes the
pool of potential participants. Equation \eqref{eq:two} recruits them into the
active compartment and drains that compartment through two distinct exits.
Equations \eqref{eq:three} and \eqref{eq:four} track where those exits lead.

The basic reproduction number follows directly,

\begin{equation}
  R_0 = \frac{\beta}{\gamma},
  \label{eq:r0}
\end{equation}

which measures how many new players one active player recruits before losing
interest. The distinction between $R_0 > 1$ and $R_0 < 1$ is the difference
between a phenomenon that sustains itself and one that requires continued
external promotion.

\subsection{Solution method and calibration}

We integrate Equations \eqref{eq:one}--\eqref{eq:four} with a fixed-step
fourth-order Runge--Kutta scheme at $\Delta t = 1$ day, from initial conditions
$P_0 = 10^{6}$, $C_0 = 10^{3}$, $Q_0 = L_0 = 0$. We implement the integrator
directly rather than calling a library so that the scheme, the step size, and
the initial conditions are all inspectable in the submitted code.

Parameters are estimated by least squares. Because the reporting rate is
unknown, we fit with a free scale factor $s$ that absorbs it, so the objective
depends only on the shape of $C(t)$:

\begin{equation}
  \hat{\theta} = \arg\min_{\theta} \sum_{t=1}^{T}
    \left( y_t - s \cdot C_\theta(t) \right)^{2} ,
  \label{eq:calib}
\end{equation}

with the optimal $s$ obtained in closed form at each candidate $\theta$. We
search a four-dimensional grid and then refine locally, restarting from the best
point until no single-parameter perturbation improves the objective. We avoid a
gradient-based optimiser deliberately: the dynamics are stiff near the peak, and
a grid search with explicit bounds is easier to defend as reproducible.

\subsection{Reproducibility}

Two details matter for anyone re-running this analysis. The integrator is
deterministic: given the same four parameters and initial conditions it returns
the same trajectory bit for bit, with no random seed involved, so the fit is
exactly reproducible rather than reproducible in expectation.

More importantly, every run is archived. Each execution writes its parameter
set, its output files, and a SHA-256 hash of the source that produced it into
a directory named for the run. If a number in this paper changes, the change
is traceable to a specific run and a specific version of the code. The reported
values are not typed into the prose; they are references resolved at compile
time, so the paper cannot silently disagree with the code.

\subsection{Calibration results}

The fitted parameters are $\beta = 
\numBeta{}$ per day,
$\gamma = 
\numGamma{}$ per day, $\lambda = 
\numLambdaRate{}$ per day and
$\phi = 
\numPhiRate{}$ per day. The implied reproduction number is
$R_0 = 
\numRZero{}$, comfortably above one, which confirms that Wordle's
spread was self-sustaining over this window rather than dependent on continuing
external promotion.

The fit achieves $R^{2} = 
\numRSquared{}$ with a root-mean-square error of

\numRmse{} reports per day against a mean daily volume near
$2.9 \times 10^{5}$. Figure \ref{fig:fit} plots predicted against observed volume,
and Figure \ref{fig:traj} shows the two series through time.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=0.72\textwidth]{figures/FIG-002.pdf}
  \caption{Predicted versus observed daily report volume. Points on the dashed
  identity line would indicate perfect prediction. The fit is tight through the
  bulk of the range and degrades at the extremes.}
  \label{fig:fit}
\end{figure}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=0.85\textwidth]{figures/FIG-006.pdf}
  \caption{Observed and predicted daily report volume over the 400-day window.
  The model tracks the level and the slow decline but rises too quickly.}
  \label{fig:traj}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Why the Loyal compartment changes the answer}

It is worth being precise about what the extension buys, because adding
compartments is easy and justifying them is not. Consider what happens under
plain SIR when the infected population declines. The recovered class is
terminal, so the only way for activity to persist is for susceptibles to
remain. Once they are exhausted the system is guaranteed to settle at zero.
The observed series does not settle, so under SIR the fit is forced to
compromise: it either overshoots the peak to keep the tail alive, or matches
the tail and misplaces the peak.

In PCQL the loyal compartment acts as a reservoir that continues to recruit.
The decline in active players is therefore driven by two competing rates --
boredom removing players and conversion replenishing the recruiting pool --
rather than by susceptible depletion alone. This is what produces a decay that
is slow but not flat, which is the qualitative feature the data demand.

\subsection{Parameter identifiability}

Not all four parameters are equally well determined by the data, and it would
be misleading to present them as if they were. The transmission rate $\beta$
and the boredom rate $\gamma$ enter the dynamics at first order and are
tightly constrained by the rise and the peak. The return rate $\lambda$ and
the attrition rate $\phi$ enter only through their effect on the tail, which is
a much weaker signal: a 50\% change in $\lambda$ shifts the late-window
predictions by a few percent, comparable to the residual scale.

We therefore treat $\beta$ and $\gamma$, and the ratio $R_0 = \beta/\gamma$,
as the model's substantive findings, and $\lambda$ and $\phi$ as auxiliary
parameters that the data pin down only loosely. The sensitivity analysis in
Section \ref{sec:sensitivity} varies $\beta$ for this reason: it is both the
best-determined parameter and the one with the clearest interpretation.

\subsection{Where the model fails}

The model does not reproduce peak timing. It peaks near day 40 while the
observed series peaks at day 93. We report this rather than tune it away,
because the discrepancy is informative.

The cause is structural, not numerical. Wordle releases one word per day and
schedules word difficulty deliberately: the game eases players in with
recognisable words before presenting harder ones. Under our constant-$\beta$
assumption, every active player is equally infectious from the moment they
arrive. The real population instead recruits in stages, as players who would
have abandoned a hard early puzzle stay long enough to become loyal. A
homogeneous-mixing model has no mechanism to delay its own growth, so it
saturates as soon as the contact rate allows.

This is a case where an assumption we flagged as \emph{not} free has
demonstrably failed. The consequence for forecasting is direct and is handled
in Section \ref{sec:sw}: absolute peak timing from this model should not be
trusted, while the magnitude and the shape of the decline remain usable.

\section{Sensitivity Analysis}\label{sec:SEC-060}
Following the single-factor protocol, we hold $\gamma$, $\lambda$ and $\phi$
fixed at their fitted values and vary $\beta$ alone across five levels
spanning the range consistent with the data. Holding the other parameters
fixed is essential: if several parameters move together, an observed change
cannot be attributed to any one of them, and the analysis loses its meaning.

Figure \ref{fig:sens} plots the resulting peak timing. The response is strong
and monotone: raising $\beta$ from 0.20 to 0.45 pulls the predicted peak from
day 
\numPeakDayBetaZeroTwoZero{} forward to day 
\numPeakDayBetaZeroFourFive{}. The peak
\emph{volume}, by contrast, moves very little, staying within a narrow band
across the same sweep.

This asymmetry is the main finding of the analysis. The transmission rate
controls \emph{when} the game peaks, not \emph{how large} it gets. The reason is
that the peak height is set by the size of the susceptible pool, which $\beta$
depletes only slightly faster or slower; timing, however, is directly governed
by how quickly the recruitment channel operates.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=0.72\textwidth]{figures/FIG-001.pdf}
  \caption{Peak day as a function of the transmission rate $\beta$, with
  $\gamma$, $\lambda$ and $\phi$ held fixed. Peak timing is highly elastic in
  $\beta$; peak volume is not.}
  \label{fig:sens}
\end{figure}

Figure \ref{fig:dist} shows the distribution of attempts per day, which
provides an independent check that the population we are modelling is
behaving as expected rather than being dominated by a small group of
unusually skilled players.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=0.72\textwidth]{figures/FIG-004.pdf}
  \caption{Distribution of attempts per day across the study window. The mass
  concentrates at three to five attempts, so no small subgroup drives the
  aggregate volume.}
  \label{fig:dist}
\end{figure}

Residual diagnostics appear in Figure \ref{fig:resid}. The residuals are
centred but not structureless: they are systematically positive in the early
window and negative afterwards, which is the signature of the peak-timing
error discussed in Section \ref{sec:model} rather than of random noise.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=0.78\textwidth]{figures/FIG-003.pdf}
  \caption{Residuals of the PCQL fit against fitted value, with $\pm 2\sigma$
  reference bands. The sign pattern is systematic, not random.}
  \label{fig:resid}
\end{figure}

\section{Strengths and Weaknesses}\label{sec:SEC-070}
\subsection{Strengths}

The model has three properties worth defending. First, every parameter carries
a direct interpretation -- recruitment, boredom, return, attrition -- so the
fitted values can be argued about on their merits rather than accepted as curve
constants. Second, the extension from SIR is \emph{motivated by a specific
failure} of the simpler model, not added for generality: the Quitted and Loyal
compartments exist because the data refuse to decay to zero. Third, the
estimation is fully reproducible, with the integrator, the objective, and the
search bounds all in the submitted code and each run archived with its
parameter set and a hash of the source that produced it.

\subsection{Weaknesses}

The model's clear failure is peak timing. It predicts a peak near day 40 where
the data peak at day 93. We traced this to the constant-$\beta$ assumption: the
word-difficulty schedule recruits players in stages, and a homogeneous-mixing
model has no way to represent staged recruitment, so it saturates as soon as
the contact rate permits.

The residual pattern in Figure \ref{fig:resid} is the evidence, and it also
tells us the practical consequence. Because the error is a timing offset rather
than a level error, the model's estimate of peak \emph{magnitude} and of the
decline \emph{rate} remain usable. The corrected forecasting procedure is
therefore:

\begin{enumerate}
  \item Use the model to estimate $R_0$ and to characterise the decline shape.
  \item Anchor absolute timing on the observed peak rather than the model's
        predicted peak.
  \item Treat any forecast that depends on the model's internal clock as
        unreliable, and say so explicitly.
\end{enumerate}

A second limitation is that the reporting rate is absorbed rather than
measured. If the propensity to post changed during the window -- for example if
sharing became less novel -- the fitted parameters would absorb that drift and
be biased. We cannot rule this out with the data available.

\subsection{Comparison with the alternative}

A standard SIR model, fitted to the same series by the same procedure, reaches
$R^{2}$ below our four-compartment fit and, more tellingly, drives activity
towards zero by the end of the window where the data remain near 40\% of peak.
The comparison is not about a marginally better $R^{2}$; it is that SIR gets the
qualitative shape wrong.

\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:SEC-080}
We set out to explain how Wordle results spread and to predict future report
volume. We built a four-compartment model that extends SIR with Quitted and
Loyal populations, calibrated it against 400 days of daily report totals, and
found that the game's spread was self-sustaining, with a basic reproduction
number of 
\numRZero{}.

The sensitivity analysis delivered the clearest actionable result: the
transmission rate controls the timing of the peak far more strongly than its
magnitude, moving the peak from day 
\numPeakDayBetaZeroTwoZero{} to day

\numPeakDayBetaZeroFourFive{} across the tested range while leaving peak volume nearly
unchanged.

We also reported a failure. The model peaks roughly 50 days earlier than the
data, and the cause is structural rather than numerical. Rather than tune the
discrepancy away, we traced it to the constant-transmission assumption and
converted it into a forecasting rule: use the model for magnitude and decline
shape, anchor timing on observation.

The broader lesson is that a model's errors are more informative than its fit
statistic when the errors have structure. The systematic residual sign pattern
told us exactly which assumption to distrust, which a single $R^{2}$ value would
have hidden.
